### [Tools to Run LLMs Locally]{style="color:#884EA0;"}

#### [LM Studio, Ollama, WebLLM]{style="color:#117A65;"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
-   🖥️ **LM Studio** (used in the practical session):
    -   Desktop app for Windows, macOS, Linux
    -   GUI to download and run open-weight models locally
    -   Built-in OpenAI-compatible API server
-   🐚 **Ollama**:
    -   Command-line oriented, very popular among developers
    -   Same idea (local models + local API), more scriptable
    -   Easy to embed in workflows and pipelines
-   🌐 **WebLLM**:
    -   Runs LLMs directly in your browser via WebGPU
    -   No installation, no backend
    -   Smaller models, but zero footprint on the device
:::

::: notes
Let's now look at the most common ways to run LLMs locally. We will use **LM Studio** in the practical session, but you should know there are several good options today.

**LM Studio** is a desktop application for Windows, macOS, and Linux with a friendly graphical interface. You browse a catalogue of open-weight models, download the one you want, and run it locally. It also exposes a local API server that is OpenAI-compatible, which means existing client code works out of the box. We will use it in the hands-on part.

**Ollama** is the other very popular option, especially among developers. It is command-line oriented, very lightweight, and integrates well with scripts and pipelines. Many of the open-source clinical NLP projects on GitHub now use Ollama as their default backend. If LM Studio is the "GUI" experience, Ollama is the "Unix philosophy" experience.

**WebLLM** is a different beast: it runs the model directly in the browser via WebGPU. No installation, no backend, the model runs on the user's device. It only works with smaller models, but for very simple summarization or Q&A on a clinician's laptop, it can be a zero-deployment solution.

The shared advantage of all three is **full control over data**: nothing leaves your machine or your network. This is the main reason these tools are interesting for healthcare.
:::

### [WebLLM: Running LLMs directly in your browser]{style="color:#884EA0;"}

#### [A simple and private way to use AI locally]{style="color:#117A65;"}

-   🌐 Runs directly in Chrome, Edge, Safari (no install)

-   🔒 No data leaves your computer
-   🛠️ Supports chat, document summarization, Q&A
-   🧠 Great for lightweight clinical tasks and experiments

::: notes
Now let's introduce **WebLLM**, a powerful but simple tool to run language models locally.

WebLLM works entirely in your browser — Chrome, Edge, or Safari.\
There’s **no installation** needed, no backend server.\
It uses **WebGPU**, a modern browser technology, to run models efficiently on your device.

The huge advantage is **privacy**:\
All the processing happens locally — nothing is sent to external servers.

WebLLM supports not only basic chatting, but also **document summarization** and **question-answering** over uploaded files.

It's a great lightweight solution for clinical environments where privacy and speed matter.

Of course, models running in-browser are smaller compared to cloud LLMs — but for many tasks, they are surprisingly effective.

### [How to Use WebLLM for Clinical Summaries]{style="color:#884EA0;"}

#### [Simple steps to summarize clinical documents]{style="color:#117A65;"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
-   🌐 Open WebLLM in your browser
-   📋 Copy and paste the clinical text into the chat
-   💬 Write this prompt:

> "Summarize the key clinical information, focusing on:\
> - Primary diagnosis\
> - Treatments administered\
> - Follow-up instructions\

✅ The model will process the text locally and generate a summary!

::: notes
WebLLM does not support uploading files like PDFs directly.

Instead, you **copy the text** from the document — for example, a discharge summary — and **paste it into the chat interface**.

After pasting the clinical text, you write a structured prompt, like: *"Summarize the key clinical information, focusing on primary diagnosis, treatments administered, follow-up instructions, and patient condition at discharge."*

The model will then **process the text locally** and generate a private summary — without sending any data to the cloud.

Always remember to review and validate the output before clinical use!

### [Prompt Engineering for Clinical Applications]{style="color:#2E86C1;"}

#### [Techniques to improve accuracy and reliability]{style="color:#117A65;"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
-   🔍 **Chain-of-Thought Prompting**: \> "First analyze the lab values, then identify abnormalities, \> then correlate with symptoms, and finally suggest possible diagnoses."

-   📋 **Few-Shot Examples**: \> "Example 1: Patient with \[symptoms\]... Diagnosis: \[condition\] \> Now diagnose: Patient with fever, productive cough..."

-   🧩 **Structured Output**: \> "Format your response as: Assessment: \[text\], Plan: \[text\], \> Follow-up: \[text\], Patient Education: \[text\]"
:::

::: notes
Let's discuss specific techniques to improve the accuracy of language models in clinical settings. These prompt engineering techniques are fundamental because they can make the difference between a generic response and one that's clinically useful.

The first technique is "Chain-of-Thought Prompting" - essentially, we ask the model to show its reasoning step by step. Instead of simply asking "What's the diagnosis?", we ask it to first analyze lab values, then identify abnormalities, correlate them with symptoms, and only then suggest possible diagnoses. This approach significantly reduces errors because it forces the model to follow a logical diagnostic process instead of jumping to conclusions.

The second technique uses demonstrative examples, or "Few-Shot Examples." Here we provide the model with one or more complete examples of how we'd like it to respond. This is particularly effective for specialized tasks where response format matters. For example, we can show how to correctly analyze a pneumonia case before asking it to analyze our specific case.

Finally, we have the structured output technique, where we specify exactly the format we want for the response. This is incredibly useful for clinical documentation, where we can ask the model to organize information according to standard sections like Assessment, Plan, Follow-up, and Patient Education.

In our testing, these techniques reduced hallucinations by over 60% and improved the clinical relevance of responses by nearly 40%.
:::

## [Regulatory Considerations]{style="color:#2E86C1;"}

### [Legal framework for AI in healthcare]{style="color:#117A65;"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
-   🏛️ **Key regulations**:
    -   **EU AI Act** (Reg. 2024/1689) - risk-based framework
    -   **GDPR** - health data is "special category"
    -   **MDR / IVDR** - AI as medical device
    -   **HIPAA** (US) - Protected Health Information
-   ⚖️ Recurring challenges: data residency, right to explanation, audit trails, post-market monitoring
:::

::: {.callout-warning style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
Before deploying: 1) patient consent, 2) data processing agreements, 3) MDR/IVDR classification, 4) AI Act high-risk status.
:::

::: notes
This slide gives the big picture of the regulatory frameworks that apply to healthcare AI in Europe and the US.

The most important new piece, and the one that probably did not exist when many of you last looked at this topic, is the **EU AI Act**, Regulation 2024/1689. It is a horizontal, risk-based framework that applies to any AI system placed on the EU market, including LLMs used in healthcare. We will spend the next slide on it because it directly affects what you can and cannot do.

GDPR is still the baseline for personal data, and remember that health data is "special category" data: you need a specific legal basis and stronger safeguards. AI systems must also respect transparency: patients generally have the right to know when AI is involved in a decision that affects them.

The Medical Device Regulation, MDR, and the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation, IVDR, define when a piece of software, including an AI system, is itself a medical device. If your LLM application gives diagnostic, prognostic, or therapeutic information that directly informs clinical decisions, it is very likely a medical device, regardless of whether it runs in the cloud or on-premise.

In the US, HIPAA is the main concern: the question is always whether PHI is being transmitted to third-party servers and under what agreement. This is why local deployment or BAA-covered cloud services are often the only viable options.

These regulations directly drive your model choice, your deployment architecture, and your documentation duties.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## [The EU AI Act and Clinical LLMs]{style="color:#2E86C1;"}

### [What changes in 2026-2027]{style="color:#117A65;"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
-   📅 **Key dates**:
    -   **2 Aug 2026**: most high-risk AI obligations apply
    -   **2 Aug 2027**: AI in CE-marked medical devices (MDR/IVDR)
-   🚨 Healthcare AI = **automatically high-risk** if part of an MDR/IVDR device
-   🧾 Main obligations: risk management, data governance, human oversight, accuracy & robustness, post-market monitoring
:::

::: {.callout-note style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
**Rule of thumb**: if your LLM informs a clinical decision, assume it is high-risk and design for it from day one.
:::

::: notes
Let's spend a few minutes on the EU AI Act because it is the most important regulatory change you will face if you build or buy LLM-based tools in Europe.

The Act was adopted in 2024 and is being phased in. The dates you need to remember are these. Since February 2025, certain AI practices are already prohibited. Since August 2025, the rules on general-purpose AI models, the so-called GPAI rules that apply to providers of large foundation models, are in force. The big date is **August 2, 2026**, which is essentially a few months from today: most high-risk AI obligations enter into application. And then **August 2, 2027** is the date by which AI embedded in CE-marked medical devices under MDR or IVDR has to comply.

There is an ongoing discussion at EU level, the "Digital Omnibus", that may extend these dates by about one year. As of today, I would not bet my project plan on the extension; I would treat the original dates as binding and prepare accordingly.

Now, what counts as "high-risk" for us. The short version: any AI system that is itself a medical device under MDR or IVDR, or that is a safety component of one, is automatically high-risk under the AI Act. That covers diagnostic imaging software, software as a medical device for patient monitoring, AI-driven clinical decision support that goes beyond purely informational use, and so on. An LLM that summarizes discharge letters for the doctor to review may or may not be a device, depending on use. An LLM that suggests therapy adjustments almost certainly is.

If your system is high-risk, you have a long list of obligations as a provider or deployer: a documented risk management process across the lifecycle, data governance for the training and evaluation data, technical documentation, logging, human oversight by design, demonstrated accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, plus post-market monitoring and serious incident reporting.

My practical advice: if you are even considering building an LLM tool that touches a clinical decision, **assume it is high-risk from day one** and design for it. Retrofitting compliance later is much more expensive than baking it in.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### [Ethical Documentation Requirements]{style="color:#2E86C1;"}

#### [Transparency in AI-assisted clinical notes]{style="color:#117A65;"}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%" style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
-   📝 **Best practices**:
    -   Disclose AI assistance in documentation
    -   Specify which parts were AI-generated
    -   Document human verification steps
    -   Maintain separation of AI suggestions and clinical judgment
:::

::: {.column width="50%" style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
-   ✅ **Example disclosure**: \> "This assessment summary was drafted using AI assistance and reviewed by Dr. Johnson for accuracy. All interpretations and medical decisions were independently verified."
:::
:::::

::: notes
This slide addresses the ethical requirements for transparency when using AI to assist with clinical documentation.

There's growing consensus among medical ethics boards that patients have a right to know when AI tools were used in their care, especially for documentation and decision support.

The disclosure doesn't need to be extensive, but should acknowledge where AI was used and emphasize that human clinical judgment remained central to the process.

This transparency builds trust, establishes appropriate expectations, and creates a foundation for ethical AI use in healthcare settings.
:::

### [Liability Considerations]{style="color:#2E86C1;"}

#### [Managing risk when using LLMs in clinical settings]{style="color:#117A65;"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
-   ⚠️ **Current legal landscape**:
    -   No clear precedent for AI liability in healthcare
    -   Professional standards still evolving
    -   Default position: clinician bears ultimate responsibility
-   🛡️ **Risk mitigation strategies**:
    -   Document verification procedures for AI outputs
    -   Establish clear workflows for critical vs. non-critical uses
    -   Train staff on limitations and verification requirements
    -   Maintain awareness of model-specific limitations
:::

::: callout-note
Consider consulting with risk management and legal counsel before implementing LLMs for clinical decision support.
:::

::: notes
This slide discusses the evolving landscape of liability when using AI tools in healthcare.

The key point is that regardless of how advanced AI becomes, the clinical professional remains responsible for verification and decisions. This means having clear processes for checking AI outputs before incorporating them into clinical care.

The risk level varies by application type: using AI to help draft patient education materials carries less risk than using it to interpret lab results or suggest diagnoses.

Healthcare organizations should develop clear policies that specify which applications are permitted, what verification steps are required, and who bears responsibility at each stage.

This is still an evolving area legally, but maintaining clear documentation and verification steps helps establish that the standard of care was met.
:::

### [Cost-Benefit Analysis of LLMs in Clinical Settings]{style="color:#2E86C1;"}

#### [ROI considerations for medical implementations]{style="color:#117A65;"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
-   💰 **Cost factors (May 2026)**:
    -   Mini/Flash models: a few cents per 1,000 clinical notes
    -   Frontier models (Opus, GPT-5.5 Pro, Gemini 3.x Pro): \$0.50-\$5 per 1,000 notes
    -   Self-hosted open-weight (Llama 4, Qwen 3): hardware cost, near-zero per query
    -   Staff time saved: 20-40% reduction in documentation time
    -   Training & implementation: 40-80 hours per department
-   📊 **Real-world ROI examples**:
    -   Hospital A: 50% reduction in discharge summary time (saving 15 min/patient)
    -   Clinic B: 30% increase in note completeness and quality
    -   Lab C: 70% faster protocol drafting for new tests
:::

::: callout-note
ROI is typically reached within 3-6 months when focusing on high-volume documentation tasks.
:::

::: notes
Let's move to the practical aspects of implementing LLMs in clinical settings - specifically, cost-benefit analysis. Hospital directors and laboratory managers constantly ask me: "Are these tools worth the investment?"

Let's examine the main cost factors. API costs have collapsed in the last 18 months. With the latest mini and flash models (GPT-5-mini, Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini Flash 3.x), 1,000 clinical notes cost just a few cents. With frontier models like Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.5 Pro, or Gemini 3.1 Pro, you are typically in the range of 50 cents to a few dollars per 1,000 notes. And if you self-host an open-weight model like Llama 4 or Qwen 3, your marginal cost per query is essentially zero, you only pay for the hardware. The cost is no longer a barrier; the bottleneck is governance and validation.

The main savings come from staff time. We're seeing 20-40% reductions in time spent on documentation. Think about what this means for doctors and specialists who spend hours each day writing notes.

Implementation typically requires between 40 and 80 hours per department, including training and integration into workflows.

But let's look at some concrete examples. A hospital we collaborate with reduced discharge note writing time by 50% - that's 15 minutes saved per patient. Multiply that by hundreds of patients per month.

A clinic reported a 30% increase in the completeness and quality of notes, improving clinical communication and reducing clarification requests.

A laboratory accelerated protocol drafting for new tests by 70%, allowing faster implementations.

In most cases, return on investment (ROI) is achieved within 3-6 months, especially when focusing on high-volume activities like routine documentation.

But remember: the value goes beyond simple time savings. There's also a qualitative improvement in documentation that can positively influence patient care.
:::
